newsitem.title: USA: Perry takes leadership blame on Saudi bombing.
newsitem.headline: Perry takes leadership blame on Saudi bombing.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Perry took the blame on Wednesday for not issuing clear orders for better security improvements before the June 25 Saudi Arabia truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. servicemen.

But Perry, at a congressional hearing, blamed one of his top commanders for the specific failure to move a security fence far enough away from the targeted military housing complex to reduce casualties and damage.
"To the extent that this tragedy resulted from a failure of leadership that responsibility is mine and mine alone," he testified at a House of Representatives National Security Committee hearing.

Perry was questioned by the committee after an official report drawn up by a retired U.S. Army general, released on Monday, blamed senior defence leaders and military commanders for failing to adequately protect Khobar Towers complex against a known, though not specific, bombing threat.
A tanker truck filled with explosives backed up against a fence near U.S. housing in the complex, blowing the front off one multi-story apartment building.

Perry said that although he had a policy requiring safeguards against terror threats, he agreed with the defence report's conclusion that senior defence leaders did not issue and emphasise clear security directives.
"I believe that that was my responsibiliy and I have changed these (policy provisions) to directives and I have taken actions to improve the emphasis on them," Perry said.

But when pressed on whether General Binford Peay III, commander of U.S. forces in the Gulf, was to blame for not moving a security fence further out from the military housing complex, Perry said he had been critical of that failure.
"There are some aspects of General Peay's performance, which I'm critical of," Perry replied. "That is one of them."
But the defence secretary said Peay "is a superb commander and he has my support. He is not perfect."
Perry said potential terrorist threats will now be the prime consideration in protecting U.S. military installations around the world.
He said an intensive survey of security improvements needed at all installations will be completed "in a matter of months, not years."
Perry repeated earlier assertions that American military installations face the threat of more attacks and must be prepared even for chemical, biological and nuclear attacks.
Perry and General John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told the committee members they are already carrying out or will consider all recommendations in Monday's report.

Perry announced earlier that these measures include creation of a new office under Shalikashvili dedicated to improving military installations' security and increasing funding for better security safeguards.
